[Textbook defect: the question describes THREE girls and Fig. 3.19 draws three paths, but the figure labels only TWO of them (A and B) — there is no "C" anywhere on it. The answer is unaffected, because the straight-line path IS one of the labelled ones, but a student is asked about a girl the figure never names.] All three girls start at \(P\) and finish at \(Q\), and displacement depends only on the end points — not on the route taken. Since \(P\) and \(Q\) are diametrically opposite, the displacement of each girl is the diameter:

\(|\text{displacement}| = 2R = 2 \times 200\,\text{m} = 400\,\text{m}\)

directed from \(P\) to \(Q\), the same for all three.

The path length equals the magnitude of the displacement only for motion along a straight line. In Fig. 3.19 only the girl on path \(B\) skates along the straight diameter \(PQ\); the other two follow curved routes that are longer than \(400\,\text{m}\).

**Displacement \(= 400\,\text{m}\) for each girl; it equals the actual path length only for girl \(B\).**

(a) The cyclist starts at the centre \(O\) and finishes at the centre \(O\). Since displacement depends only on the end points,

**net displacement \(= 0\)**

(b) Average velocity \(= \dfrac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{0}{10\,\text{min}}\)

**average velocity \(= 0\)**

(c) The path is \(OP\) (a radius), then the arc \(PQ\), then \(QO\) (a radius). From Fig. 3.20, \(OP\) and \(OQ\) are perpendicular, so arc \(PQ\) is a quarter of the circumference:

arc \(PQ = \tfrac{1}{4}(2\pi R) = \tfrac{\pi}{2} \times 1\,\text{km} = 1.571\,\text{km}\)

Total path length \(= 1 + 1.571 + 1 = 3.571\,\text{km}\)

Time \(= 10\,\text{min} = \tfrac{1}{6}\,\text{h}\)

Average speed \(= \dfrac{3.571\,\text{km}}{(1/6)\,\text{h}} = 21.4\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)

**(a) \(0\)  (b) \(0\)  (c) \(21.4\,\text{km h}^{-1}\) (\(= 5.95\,\text{m s}^{-1}\))**

Each straight run is \(500\,\text{m}\) and the track turns left through \(60^{\circ}\) at every turn, so the successive displacement vectors are equal in magnitude and each is rotated \(60^{\circ}\) from the previous one. The motorist therefore traces a **regular hexagon** of side \(500\,\text{m}\) (six turns close the path).

Taking the first run along the \(x\)-axis, the \(k\)-th run is \(500\left(\cos 60k^{\circ}\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \sin 60k^{\circ}\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\right)\,\text{m}\), with \(k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)

**Third turn** — sum of the first three runs \(= (500\,\hat{\mathbf{i}}) + (250\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 433\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}) + (-250\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 433\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = 500\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 866\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\,\text{m}\)

\(|\text{displacement}| = \sqrt{500^{2} + 866^{2}} = 1000\,\text{m}\), at \(60^{\circ}\) to the initial direction. (This is the long diagonal of the hexagon, \(= 2 \times 500\,\text{m}\).) Path length \(= 3 \times 500 = 1500\,\text{m}\); ratio \(= 1000/1500 = 0.67\).

**Sixth turn** — six runs complete the hexagon and bring him back to the start.

\(|\text{displacement}| = 0\). Path length \(= 3000\,\text{m}\); ratio \(= 0\).

**Eighth turn** — eight runs \(=\) one full hexagon plus two more runs, so the displacement is that of the first two runs:

\(500\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + (250\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 433\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = 750\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 433\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\,\text{m}\)

\(|\text{displacement}| = \sqrt{750^{2} + 433^{2}} = 866\,\text{m}\), at \(30^{\circ}\) to the initial direction. Path length \(= 4000\,\text{m}\); ratio \(= 0.22\).

**Third turn: \(1000\,\text{m}\) at \(60^{\circ}\) to the start direction (path \(1500\,\text{m}\)). Sixth turn: \(0\) (path \(3000\,\text{m}\)). Eighth turn: \(866\,\text{m}\) at \(30^{\circ}\) to the start direction (path \(4000\,\text{m}\)). The magnitude of the displacement is always less than the path length, and the gap widens as the motorist goes round.**

Time \(= 28\,\text{min} = \dfrac{28}{60}\,\text{h}\)

(a) Average speed uses the actual path length, \(23\,\text{km}\):

\(\text{average speed} = \dfrac{23\,\text{km}}{28/60\,\text{h}} = 49.3\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)

(b) The magnitude of the average velocity uses the displacement, which is the straight-line separation of station and hotel, \(10\,\text{km}\):

\(|\text{average velocity}| = \dfrac{10\,\text{km}}{28/60\,\text{h}} = 21.4\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)

The two are **not** equal, because the cabman's path (\(23\,\text{km}\)) is longer than the displacement (\(10\,\text{km}\)). They would be equal only if he had driven straight along the \(10\,\text{km}\) road.

**(a) \(49.3\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)  (b) \(21.4\,\text{km h}^{-1}\); they are not equal.**

The ball must just graze the ceiling, so its maximum height equals the height of the hall. For a projectile thrown at \(\theta\) with speed \(v_o\),

\(H = \dfrac{v_o^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{2g}\)

Setting \(H = 25\,\text{m}\), \(v_o = 40\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\):

\(\sin^{2}\theta = \dfrac{2gH}{v_o^{2}} = \dfrac{2 \times 9.8 \times 25}{40^{2}} = \dfrac{490}{1600} = 0.3063\)

\(\sin\theta = 0.5534\), so \(\theta = 33.6^{\circ}\) and \(\cos\theta = 0.8329\).

The horizontal distance is the range at this angle:

\(R = \dfrac{v_o^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2 v_o^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2 \times 1600 \times 0.5534 \times 0.8329}{9.8}\)

\(R = 150.5\,\text{m}\)

Throwing at any larger angle would send the ball through the ceiling; any smaller angle gives a shorter range.

**Maximum horizontal distance \(= 150.5\,\text{m}\) (thrown at about \(33.6^{\circ}\) to the horizontal).**

The maximum horizontal range is obtained at \(\theta = 45^{\circ}\), where \(\sin 2\theta = 1\):

\(R_{\max} = \dfrac{v_o^{2}}{g} = 100\,\text{m}\)

so \(v_o^{2} = 100\,g\).

The ball goes highest when thrown vertically upward with that same speed \(v_o\). Using \(v^{2} = v_o^{2} - 2gH\) with \(v = 0\) at the top,

\(H = \dfrac{v_o^{2}}{2g} = \dfrac{100\,g}{2g} = 50\,\text{m}\)

The result is independent of \(g\) — the maximum height is always half the maximum range.

**\(H = 50\,\text{m}\)**

The stone moves in a horizontal circle of radius \(R = 80\,\text{cm} = 0.80\,\text{m}\) at constant speed, so this is uniform circular motion.

Frequency \(\nu = \dfrac{14}{25}\,\text{s}^{-1} = 0.56\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Angular speed \(\omega = 2\pi\nu = 2\pi \times 0.56 = 3.52\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\)

The acceleration is centripetal:

\(a = \omega^{2}R = (3.52)^{2} \times 0.80 = 9.9\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)

(As a check, \(v = \omega R = 2.81\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(a = v^{2}/R = 2.81^{2}/0.80 = 9.9\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).)

Its direction is along the string, from the stone towards the centre of the circle, and it changes continuously as the stone goes round.

**\(a = 9.9\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), directed radially inwards (along the string, towards the centre).**

Convert to SI:

\(v = 900\,\text{km h}^{-1} = \dfrac{900 \times 1000}{3600} = 250\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(R = 1.00\,\text{km} = 1000\,\text{m}\)

The centripetal acceleration is

\(a_c = \dfrac{v^{2}}{R} = \dfrac{(250)^{2}}{1000} = 62.5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)

Comparing with \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\):

\(\dfrac{a_c}{g} = \dfrac{62.5}{9.8} = 6.4\)

**\(a_c = 62.5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), about \(6.4\) times the acceleration due to gravity.**

The statement holds only for **uniform** circular motion, where the speed is constant and the whole acceleration is the centripetal one, \(v^{2}/R\), pointing at the centre.

If the speed changes — a stone whirled faster and faster, a car speeding up on a circular track — there is also a **tangential** acceleration \(\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}t\) along the direction of motion. The net acceleration is then the vector sum of a radial and a tangential part, and it is not directed along the radius.

The word **always** is what makes the statement wrong.

**False.**

Velocity is defined as \(\mathbf{v} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\dfrac{\Delta\mathbf{r}}{\Delta t}\).

As \(\Delta t \to 0\) the chord \(\Delta\mathbf{r}\) joining two nearby points on the path turns into the tangent at that point. So the instantaneous velocity is always directed along the tangent to the trajectory, whatever the shape of the path and whether or not the speed is changing.

**True.**

The average acceleration over an interval is

\(\mathbf{a}_{\text{av}} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_f - \mathbf{v}_i}{\Delta t}\)

After exactly one cycle the particle is back at its starting point moving with the same speed in the same direction, so \(\mathbf{v}_f = \mathbf{v}_i\) and \(\mathbf{v}_f - \mathbf{v}_i = 0\). Hence \(\mathbf{a}_{\text{av}} = 0\).

Equivalently, the centripetal acceleration has constant magnitude but points towards the centre from every point of the circle; over a full cycle these directions are distributed symmetrically and cancel in pairs.

Note this is the average of the acceleration **vector**; the magnitude of the acceleration is \(v^{2}/R\) at every instant and is never zero.

**True.**

(a) Differentiate the position vector with respect to time:

\(\mathbf{v} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(3.0t\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 2.0t^{2}\,\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 4.0\,\hat{\mathbf{k}}\right) = 3.0\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4.0t\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d}t} = -4.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)

The acceleration is constant, of magnitude \(4.0\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), directed along the \(-y\) direction.

(b) At \(t = 2.0\,\text{s}\):

\(\mathbf{v} = 3.0\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 8.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{3.0^{2} + 8.0^{2}} = \sqrt{73} = 8.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{|v_y|}{v_x}\right) = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{8.0}{3.0}\right) = 69.4^{\circ}\)

Since \(v_x > 0\) and \(v_y < 0\), this angle is measured **below** the \(x\)-axis.

**(a) \(\mathbf{v} = 3.0\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4.0t\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), \(\mathbf{a} = -4.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)  (b) \(8.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), at \(69.4^{\circ}\) below the \(x\)-axis (i.e. \(-69.4^{\circ}\) from the \(+x\) direction).**

The motion has constant acceleration, so \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{v}_o t + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^{2}\) with \(\mathbf{r}_o = 0\), \(\mathbf{v}_o = 10.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(\mathbf{a} = (8.0\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 2.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). In components,

\(x(t) = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(8.0)t^{2} = 4.0t^{2}\)

\(y(t) = 10.0t + \tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)t^{2} = 10.0t + t^{2}\)

(a) Setting \(x = 16\,\text{m}\):

\(4.0t^{2} = 16 \Rightarrow t^{2} = 4 \Rightarrow t = 2.0\,\text{s}\)

At that instant \(y = 10.0(2.0) + (2.0)^{2} = 24\,\text{m}\)

(b) The velocity is \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}_o + \mathbf{a}t\):

\(\mathbf{v} = 10.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}} + (8.0\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 2.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}})(2.0) = 16.0\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 14.0\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{16.0^{2} + 14.0^{2}} = \sqrt{452} = 21.3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

**(a) \(t = 2.0\,\text{s}\), \(y = 24\,\text{m}\)  (b) speed \(= 21.3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)**

**Magnitudes and directions.**

\(|\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}}| = \sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{2} = 1.41\), at \(\tan^{-1}(1/1) = 45^{\circ}\) to the \(x\)-axis.

\(|\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}}| = \sqrt{1^{2} + (-1)^{2}} = \sqrt{2} = 1.41\), at \(45^{\circ}\) **below** the \(x\)-axis (i.e. \(-45^{\circ}\)).

**Components of \(\mathbf{A} = 2\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}\).** The component of \(\mathbf{A}\) along a direction is \(\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), where \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is the unit vector along it.

Along \(\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}}\): \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_1 = \dfrac{\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}}}{\sqrt{2}}\), so

\(\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_1 = \dfrac{2 + 3}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}} = 3.54\)

Along \(\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}}\): \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_2 = \dfrac{\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}}}{\sqrt{2}}\), so

\(\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_2 = \dfrac{2 - 3}{\sqrt{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = -0.71\)

The negative sign means this component points opposite to \(\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}}\). As a check, \(\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_2 = \tfrac{5}{2}(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}) - \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = 2\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3\,\hat{\mathbf{j}} = \mathbf{A}\).

**Both \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) have magnitude \(\sqrt{2}\), at \(45^{\circ}\) above and \(45^{\circ}\) below the \(x\)-axis respectively. The components of \(\mathbf{A}\) are \(5/\sqrt{2} = 3.54\) along \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) and \(-1/\sqrt{2} = -0.71\) along \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}\).**

The average velocity is defined as displacement divided by time, and there is no general reason why it should equal the arithmetic mean of the velocities at the two end instants.

That mean is correct only for **uniformly accelerated** motion, where \(\mathbf{v}\) varies linearly with \(t\). For arbitrary motion the relation fails — for example, a particle that speeds up and slows down between \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) may have identical velocities at both instants, making the right-hand side equal to \(\mathbf{v}(t_1)\) while the true average velocity is quite different.

**False (true only for constant acceleration).**

This **is** the definition of average velocity: the displacement \(\mathbf{r}(t_2) - \mathbf{r}(t_1)\) divided by the time interval \(t_2 - t_1\).

A definition carries no assumption about how the velocity or acceleration varies, so it holds for any motion whatsoever.

**True (valid for any arbitrary motion).**

This kinematic relation is obtained by integrating \(\mathbf{a} = \mathrm{d}\mathbf{v}/\mathrm{d}t\) while treating \(\mathbf{a}\) as a constant that can be taken outside the integral.

If the acceleration varies with time the integral gives \(\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{v}(0) + \int_0^t \mathbf{a}\,\mathrm{d}t'\) instead, which is not \(\mathbf{a}t\).

**False (true only for constant acceleration).**

This relation follows from integrating the velocity twice with the acceleration held constant, so it presupposes uniform acceleration.

For arbitrary motion the acceleration cannot be taken outside the integral and the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^{2}\) term is not valid; uniform circular motion is a familiar counter-example, where \(\mathbf{a}\) has constant magnitude but continuously changing direction.

**False (true only for constant acceleration).**

This **is** the definition of average acceleration: the change in velocity divided by the time interval over which it occurs.

Being a definition, it assumes nothing about the motion and holds in general.

**True (valid for any arbitrary motion).**

Being conserved is neither necessary nor sufficient for a quantity to be a scalar.

Not necessary: temperature, density and speed are scalars that are certainly not conserved — a body cools, a gas is compressed, a car brakes.

Not sufficient: linear momentum and angular momentum are conserved in an isolated system, yet both are vectors.

**False.**

Many scalars are routinely negative. Temperature on the Celsius scale can be \(-10\,^{\circ}\text{C}\); the gravitational potential energy of a bound pair is negative; electric charge can be negative; work done by friction is negative.

The sign of a scalar carries physical meaning; it is not forbidden.

**False.**

A scalar is specified by a magnitude **together with its unit**, and most scalars carry dimensions — mass (\(\text{kg}\)), energy (\(\text{J}\)), density (\(\text{kg m}^{-3}\)), temperature (\(\text{K}\)).

Some scalars are dimensionless (refractive index, coefficient of friction, strain), but that is a property of those particular quantities, not a requirement for being a scalar.

**False.**

A scalar may perfectly well be a function of position — such a quantity is called a scalar field.

The temperature inside a room varies from point to point, as do the density of the atmosphere with altitude and the gravitational potential around the Earth; all three are scalars.

**False.**

This is precisely the defining property of a scalar: it is **invariant under a rotation of the coordinate axes**.

A scalar is fixed by a single number and needs no reference to axes at all, so two observers whose axes are differently oriented must record the same value — the mass of a body, or the magnitude of a vector, does not change when you turn your axes. The components of a vector, by contrast, do change.

**True.**

The aircraft flies horizontally at a constant height \(h = 3400\,\text{m}\). Let the observer on the ground be at \(O\), and let the two positions \(10.0\,\text{s}\) apart subtend the angle \(\angle AOB = 30^{\circ}\) at \(O\). Taking the flight path symmetric about the vertical through \(O\), the vertical bisects the angle, giving two right triangles each with half-angle

\(\dfrac{\theta}{2} = 15^{\circ}\)

In each right triangle the horizontal distance from the foot of the vertical is

\(h\tan 15^{\circ}\)

so the distance flown in \(10.0\,\text{s}\) is

\(AB = 2h\tan 15^{\circ} = 2 \times 3400 \times 0.2679 = 1822\,\text{m}\)

The speed is therefore

\(v = \dfrac{AB}{t} = \dfrac{1822\,\text{m}}{10.0\,\text{s}} = 182\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

**\(v = 182\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) (about \(656\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)).**
